p: Please see tutorial at https://sandialabs.github.io/InterSpec/tutorials/rel_eff_peaks/20220922_InterSpec_RelEff_Peaks_SAND2022_15323TR.pdf for use instructions.

The peaks you fit are usually far more precise than the relative efficiency model that is fit through them. A high-statistics peak may be measured to a few tenths of a percent, while the efficiency curve typically only describes the data to a few percent, so that peak can sit many statistical sigma from the fitted curve without anything being wrong with the peak. This is why the χ2/DOF shown with the results is often large - it is comparing the model against counting statistics alone.
The "Add. Uncert" option controls how the peaks are weighted against each other, and how the uncertainties you are shown are arrived at:

ul.li: Stat. Only (default): each peak is weighted by its own counting statistics. If the peaks scatter about the fitted curve by more than their uncertainties allow, the reported uncertainties are widened to reflect the scatter actually observed. The widening is based on the typical (median) peak, so one or two badly mis-fit peaks do not inflate everything - if any peak is more than three sigma from the curve it is instead named in a warning, since re-fitting that peak is usually the real fix.

Auto: identical fitted values to Stat. Only, but the widening is applied to each peak's uncertainty before fitting rather than to the final answer, so it is visible in the chart's error bars and is stated with the results. Every peak is scaled by the same factor, which is why the fit itself does not move.

Strict Stat.: the purely statistical uncertainty, as if the efficiency model were exactly correct. On real spectra this is usually much too small - use it only when a statistics-only figure is specifically what you want.

1% - 100%: adds a fixed uncertainty proportional to each peak's area. This changes how peaks are weighted relative to each other, taking influence away from the high-statistics peaks. Tested against certified uranium reference materials, this shifts the fitted enrichment downward - by roughly 0.2 to 2 percentage points, growing with the percentage and levelling off around 25%. Keep this in mind if you use these settings.
Unweighted: every peak contributes equally, regardless of its statistical uncertainty.

p: On the chart, the data-point error bars and the shaded band around the fitted curve are both 1-sigma. The point error bars are statistical only.

Each nuclide panel has a Profile uncert. check-box. When checked, that nuclide's uncertainty is found by pushing the quantity away from its fitted value while every other quantity is re-fit around it, and reading off where the χ2 has risen by the amount corresponding to 68.3% and 95.4% confidence. The quantity scanned is the nuclide's mass fraction of its element when the element has more than one isotope in the problem, and otherwise its relative activity.

This gives an asymmetric interval, and unlike the usual uncertainty it stays meaningful when the answer is near a physical bound (0% or 100% for a fraction, zero for an activity), or when the problem is poorly constrained - situations where a symmetric ± is misleading. Each step starts from the solution the fit already found, so it typically costs 6 to 8 extra fits - well under a second. Results appear in the chart title and beneath the mass-fraction table.

A note on relative activities with the empirical equation forms (everything except FRAM Physical): there, only the product of the efficiency curve and the activities is determined by the data, and the split between them is set by the convention that the average measured relative efficiency is 1. The profile respects that convention, so the interval is a valid uncertainty on the reported activity - but if what you want is a quantity free of any convention, use a ratio of two activities. With FRAM Physical the detector response sets the absolute scale, so this caveat does not apply.
